My first powerhouse instant-ramen recipe
Made this as a way to really make something out of instant ramen.

Ingredients:
- 3-4 ramen packs (different flavors)
- a bag of mixed greens (lettuce and whatnot from Tesco)
- a sausage jar (anything you like will do)
- vegetable oil
- soy sauce
- Worcestershire sauce
- brown sugar
- spicy oil (optional)

Prep:
1- boil water in a casserole and make the instant noodles as you would usually
2- add soy sauce and brown sugar (half a tsp) and mix
3- in a large pan, cut up the sausages and stir fry them with Worcestershire sauce
4- once the sausages are almost done add the mixed greens (as much as you want) in the pan and mix.
5- dump the noodles in the pan and mix everything
6- (optional) top with some spicy oil

And that's it! Quite easy to make and very tasty honestly. What do you guys think?

Not sure if anyone has done this before but ramp guacamole is fantastic!
I live in the northeastern US (Connecticut specifically) and late April/ early May is ramp season. If you're not familiar, ramps are a leafy plant in the allium family (garlic and onions are also members). They are not easily cultivated and are foraged wild as they pop up. Their range extends down the eastern US from Virginia to New Hampshire. Ramps tend to grow on well drained slopes in partially shaded areas. Roadside and margins adjacent to fields are common places to find them along with banks leading down to streams in wooded areas. [They have broad elongated leaves with 2 (sometimes 3) leaves sharing a stem.](https://i.imgur.com/m2PUmvk.jpg)

A quick note on foraging; in order to preserve the plant for following seasons, it's important to only take one leaf from the plant and to preferentially harvest the outer leaf from 3 leaf plants. Ramps grow and spread very slowly so an overzealous forager can wipe out an entire patch. Don't be that person.

Now, if you're lucky enough to find some ramps near you, it's time to cook with them. Ramps have a delicate flavor that is reminiscent of green onions and garlic, but I swear there's a component to their flavor that's all their own. Typically the leaves are minced like other herbs and used in compound butter or in sauces. They can be a bit harsh raw (unless you're making ramp guacamole!) but I still enjoy a sprinkling on a finished dish or pizza, just don't go overboard.

Onto the main event. I really love guacamole (shocker), and one of my favorite ways to make it is to add a tiny amount of mashed, pasted fresh garlic. It adds to the earthy, savory flavor of the avocados and elevates it, especially when paired with something simple like tortilla chips or carrots. This was the genesis of ramp guacamole.

Since ramps provide both an oniony, vegetal flavor along with a hint of garlic, they seemed a perfect accompaniment to avocados. Not only was I right about this, but there's something about their unique flavor that, to me, pairs perfectly with the extra fatty spring avocados. So, without further adieu, the recipe.

[Ramp Guacamole](https://i.imgur.com/8KO6DVA.jpg)

Ingredients:

* 3 ripe avocados

* healthy handful of ramp leaves (6-8, more if you like it like I do), minced

* 1 tablespoon minced cilantro

* juice of one half of a lime (plus more to taste)

* salt and pepper to taste

----------------------------------------

1. Cube avocados and add into medium bowl

2. Add ramps and cilantro

3. Add lime juice and healthy starting amount of salt and pepper (i usually might start with a 1/4 tsp of salt, but will often add more)

4. Mix, mash and taste, adding more lime juice and salt as necessary to balance

5. Serve immediately or for best flavor, let sit at room temperature for about 30 min.

It's hard to describe the flavor as compared to regular oniony guacamole except to say that it seems deeper and more complex. The ramps don't add crunch so the blend is perfectly smooth. I do enjoy the crunch of red onion in guac, but the smoothness is a pleasant change and it's so freaking good I think I don't care.

So good hunting to those lucky enough to live near ramps, and if you do, give this recipe a try. It's a great seasonal treat!

Help with locating my bitter taste? 
Howdy Hey r/Cooking!

I was hoping someone could lend a bit of a hand here, as I need some help narrowing down what I might have done wrong on my soup last night. 

I was getting ready to make Zuppa Tuscana, and noticed I was out of Dillweed so I headed to the store. While I was there, I finally found some smoked paprika I had been looking for, and got that along side my Dill. 

Normally I make my own veggie broth with left over scraps, so I did that as usual. The scraps included bits of onions, carrots, and celery. I also added a bit of garlic, salt, and chicken bullion powder. I also added one extra onion just for some extra volume as I didn't have too much scrap to work with. Lastly, I also wanted to spice it up a bit and added two small lemons whole (cut in half with the rinds and all) 

I think this may have been my mistake? I simmered everything like normal for about two hours and strained through a fine mesh. I didn't taste it, as usually veggie broth is not too good on its own (just for my taste though). My wife tasted it, and said if was different but not too bad. She could definitely taste the lemon. 

When making the soup, I did the normal steps, but added smoked paprika, as I really wanted to try it out. Only added about a tablespoon to start. I also added a little more cream than I normally do, as we were almost out.(Nornally use 1 cup, used 1 1/3 cup this time) When finished with the soup, we had about 8 or so cups total. This is just so everyone knows the ratio of lemon-smoked paprika-liquid.

When the soup was done, I sprinkled a little bit of red pepper for myself into my bowl, took a nice big bite thinking I would get this glorious mouthful of creamy Italian sausage goodness with that new smoked paprika hint. I had an oberhwleminf sensation of flavor that was magnificent... For about 3 seconds.

Then a flood of a disgusting bitter aftertaste that I can only describe as... Like chewing a leaf from a fresh bush outside.

I was able to save it by adding a lot of Tony Chac Creole seasoning and then adding a cup of water and milk. The bitterness was still there, but it was more managable. 

With the limited information I have provided, could anyone possibly help me discover what might have ruined my favorite bowl of goodness? Was is the paprika that I wasn't ready for? Did the lemon rinds/peel ruin my veggie stock? Was my kale bad? I am at a complete loss and just looking for a bit of input.

Sure! Here's a simple recipe to make guacamole inspired by Chipotle's famous version using the ingredients you've provided:

### Ingredients:
- 2 ripe Hass avocados
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped cilantro
- 2 tablespoons finely diced red onions
- 2 teaspoons finely chopped jalapeños (adjust to taste for spiciness)
- 2 tablespoons citrus juice (you can use lime or a mix of lime and lemon)
- 1/2 teaspoon of salt (adjust to taste)

### Instructions:

1. **Prepare the Avocados**: Cut the avocados in half and remove the pits. Scoop the avocado flesh into a bowl.

2. **Mash the Avocado**: Use a fork or potato masher to lightly mash the avocado to your preferred consistency. Some people like it chunky, and others prefer it smoother.

3. **Add the Flavors**: Add the finely chopped cilantro, diced red onions, chopped jalapeños, and salt to the bowl with the mashed avocado.

4. **Citrus Juice**: Squeeze in the citrus juice. This not only adds flavor but also helps prevent the guacamole from browning.

5. **Mix It Up**: Gently stir everything together until well combined. Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt or citrus juice if necessary.

6. **Serve**: Enjoy your guacamole immediately, served with tortilla chips, or as a side to your favorite dishes.

### Tips:
- **Choosing Avocados**: Make sure your avocados are ripe for the best flavor and texture. They should feel slightly soft when gently squeezed.
- **Citrus Juice**: Lime juice is traditional in guacamole and offers a bright, tangy flavor, but lemon juice or a mix can add a unique twist.
- **Adjusting Heat**: The heat level can be adjusted by using more or less jalapeño. Removing the seeds and veins from the jalapeños can also reduce the heat.

This recipe closely follows the simplicity and freshness of Chipotle's guacamole, focusing on high-quality ingredients and straightforward preparation. Enjoy!

The noodles are coated in a savory, sweet, sesame oil and minced garlic sauce, and served with juicy umami mushrooms, julienned cucumber and a boiled egg. Sprinkle the noodles with toasted sesame seeds and chopped scallions to finish. These Korean soy sauce noodles can be made in 15 minutes so they’re the perfect quick and easy summer dish.   

Other popular toppings include carrots, zucchini, cold meat, and salad vegetables. I also like avocado too.   

INGREDIENTS:  
Noodles  
\* 7 oz (200g) wheat noodles (Thin pasta/somyeon noodles)- I used vermicelli pasta

\* Mushrooms  
\* 4 garlic cloves, minced  
\* 5 mushrooms (2 cups chopped/150g)  
\* 2 tbsp soy sauce  
\* 2 tbsp sugar  
\* 2 tbsp sesame oil  
\* cracked black pepper  

More Toppings  
\* 1-2 boiled eggs  
\* cucumber  
\* scallions, chopped  
\* toasted sesame seeds  

INSTRUCTIONS:  
1. Boil 1-2 eggs; 4 minutes=soft-boiled, and 9 minutes=hard-boiled eggs. Peel and set aside.  
2. Add oil to a pan and sauté 4 minced garlic cloves, then add sliced 5 mushrooms, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 2 tbsp sugar, 2 tbsp sesame oil, and cracked black pepper.   
3. Cook 7 oz (200g) thin pasta/Korean somyeon noodles according to package instructions. Rinse the noodles well under a running tap to removed excess milky starch. Drain well.   
4. Mix the noodles in the pan of saucy mushrooms (unless you want the mushrooms arranged on top of the noodles, as pictured). Plate up.  
5. Add matchstick cucumbers, boiled egg, chopped scallions and toasted sesame seeds.
